ACTING CHAIR ( Senator Grogan ): Good morning, everybody. I declare open this hearing of the Community Affairs Legislation Committee into budget estimates 2026-27. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today. I pay my respects to their elders, past, present and emerging, and extend those respects to anyone in the room or joining us today online who is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander descent. The committee has set Friday 24 July as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice, and the committee would ask senators to provide any written questions on notice to the secretariat by Friday 12 June.

The committee's proceedings today will begin with the Department of Social Services whole-of-portfolio and corporate matters. The committee will be conducting today's hearing in person and via videoconference. Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance for questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purposes of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has resolved that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policy or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, and I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

ACTING CHAIR: I would now like to welcome Senator the Hon. Anthony Chisholm, Assistant Minister for Regional Development and Assistant Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, representing the Minister for Social Services. Minister, would you care to make an opening statement?

Senator Chisholm: No, thanks, Chair, but it's good to be back again.

ACTING CHAIR: Thank you for joining us today. We really do appreciate you taking the time. I'd also like to welcome secretary of the department, Mr Michael Lye. Would you care to make an opening statement?

Mr Lye : No.

ACTING CHAIR: Welcome. Thanks for coming along today. We are going to whole-of-portfolio and corporate matters, and we will start with Senator Ruston.

Senator RUSTON: That's because there's no-one else here. Welcome, Mr Lye. Nice to see you. My understanding is that the committee wrote to you on 22 May, and you responded on 28 May, in relation to providing early access to data that the committee members had sought to prosecute issues in relation to today. You wrote back and you made the comment in your letter that the department recognises the importance of accountability to the Senate, so I acknowledge that. But in your letter, after making that comment, you then wrote, 'Given the effort required to compile the balance of the information sought in your requested timeframe, we consider it more effective to focus our efforts on preparing for discussion for the hearings today.' I put it to you, Mr Lye, that you don't actually get to decide that. This committee of the Senate has requested that information, so I'm keen to understand if you have a more substantial reason as to why you refused to provide the information that was requested of the department.

Senator Chisholm: Can I make a point?

Senator RUSTON: Sure.

Senator Chisholm: My understanding of the letter is that it wasn't from the committee; it was from Senator Askew.

Senator RUSTON: Yes, that's correct. Nonetheless, I'll give you another example. A very similar letter was addressed via the committee to another hearing, and we got the same answer.

ACTING CHAIR: Was that an estimates hearing?

Senator RUSTON: Yes, but my point is we have a choice here. We can take this matter to the floor of the chamber. Quite frankly, I think you'd have to agree the prosecution of questioning this week in this committee has been entirely friendly and respectful. The request for this information is actually to save time so that we're able to go through the information. So, we've got a choice: we can either prosecute these issues here, through frustration, and then next time we take it to the floor of the Senate and demand that this information is released, or we can play respectfully and provide the information. I'd just like it on the record, Mr Lye—and I'll make sure it's communicated to other secretaries—that we don't ask for this information for no reason. It actually helps us in the delivery of our prosecution for transparency through estimates. I would suggest, respectfully, that maybe if you provided it next time it would save us having to take it to the floor of the Senate and make a public spectacle of the fact that departments are refusing to provide information that senators are reasonably asking for. I don't intend to prosecute it anymore, but I draw to your attention that the Senate has primacy over everything.

Senator Chisholm: I'm happy for the secretary to respond if he wants to. I'd make two points. Firstly, I'd reinforce that it did come from Senator Askew directly, not from the committee. Secondly, I've been around the estimates process a bit. I've seen different approaches from departments. I'm aware of some instances where people have written in and the secretary has written back in a similar way, saying they're here to answer questions today. I don't think there is a uniform approach to it that I've observed. I know that some may do that, but traditionally, from what I have seen, when that has happened it's come through the committee, not from an individual senator.

Senator RUSTON: If there had been a concern that it had only come from an individual senator, I would respectfully suggest that maybe you should have said so. Nonetheless, the issue that I have, and I think we have more generally, is that Senate estimates are around transparency and scrutiny. I would suggest that, to an outsider looking in, refusing to provide information—

Senator Chisholm: That's—

Senator RUSTON: Can I just finish—in a sense, would look like that transparency and scrutiny were being restricted in some way. That's all I'm saying.

Senator Chisholm: That's an inaccurate assessment because the secretary, in my understanding, clearly said he's going to prepare to answer questions today. So far you've wasted five minutes on this rather than asking a question.

Senator RUSTON: I think actually drawing attention to the fact that there is a lack of transparency—

Senator Chisholm: That's not true. They are here, ready to answer questions, but you're not asking any.

Senator RUSTON: is not wasting time.

Senator Chisholm: You're not actually asking any questions.

Senator RUSTON: I think I'm making a very significant point about the lack of transparency of your government.

Senator Chisholm: That's completely outrageous. You might be making a point in your own mind; it's not resonating with anyone else.

ACTING CHAIR: I don't think that it is a fair characterisation to say the department has refused. What they said is they were prepared on the basis of your letter and have come here ready to answer the questions.

Senator RUSTON: I'm happy to move on. My point has been made. Could I ask some questions around benefit restriction notices.

Mr Lye : Yes, but benefit restriction notices is part of outcome 1.

Senator RUSTON: I'm happy to leave it to outcome 1.

Mr Lye : Yes. We might have the relevant officers here for that.

Senator RUSTON: I'll file that one to the next one. Could I ask about APS staffing issues.

Mr Lye : Yes.

Senator RUSTON: I'm keen to understand whether the department has implemented a freeze on employment.

Ms Connolly : No, we don't have a freeze on employment. About 12 months ago, though, the department took steps to curtail the external recruitment that it was undertaking. We were in a situation where our resourcing was above our appropriation. We had a net cash operating loss in 2024-25 of $6.8 million. We are in a similar situation this financial year, so that constraint has continued, but we have also continued to recruit externally where we have needed to.

Senator RUSTON: Was the decision to curtail recruitment made by the department?

Ms Connolly : Yes.

Senator RUSTON: When was this? You said this decision was made 12 months ago.

Ms Connolly : It was about 12 months ago, potentially slightly more—maybe 14 months ago.

Senator RUSTON: How many staff vacancies are there at the moment in the department?

Ms Connolly : We are in a situation where we have about the right number of staff for our funding.

Senator RUSTON: I think my question was more around if you have the staff that are required to fill the positions. Are you actively seeking to employ? Not all staff can do all jobs.

Ms Connolly : That's fair. We have a number of external vacancies that are either advertised or about to be advertised. I think it'll be in the order of 20 or so. We also have a very active program of internal expressions of interest so that staff can be moved to priority areas. If they feel, for their own development, they would like to do something different, they put up their hand and we consider internal expressions of interest first, before advertising externally.

Senator RUSTON: If it would be possible for the 20 positions that you aren't filling or intending to fill internally, could you give us a breakdown of the APS levels.

Ms Connolly : I'll need to take that on notice. I can get back to you today on that.

Mr Lye : We publish that.

Senator RUSTON: That's fine. I didn't expect you to have that with you. Has there been any direction given to you by the minister to reduce numbers?

Mr Lye : No.

Ms Connolly : No.

Senator RUSTON: Has any program of voluntary redundancies been put in place?

Ms Connolly : Yes. Following the restriction of external recruitment as well as a number of other measures in the department to reduce our expenditure, some of which were successful, we did find that we were still in a situation where our staffing exceeded our resources not only for this year but also, importantly, for our forecast for next year. The department has conducted a call for expressions of interest for voluntary redundancies over the period of December to February. We expect to issue 312 voluntary redundancies this financial year as a result of normal management but also that call for expressions of interest.

Senator RUSTON: Can I clarify—and it might just be a matter of nomenclature. When I asked the first question, you described the action the department was taking as curtailing recruitment. Then, in your response to that question, you said 'following the restriction of external recruitment'. Are they the same thing?

Ms Connolly : Yes, they are.

Senator RUSTON: Is the voluntary redundancy call still open?

Ms Connolly : No, not the expressions of interest process.

Senator RUSTON: How was the voluntary redundancy communicated to your workforce?

Ms Connolly : There was an all-staff communication. I should say the process was conducted in consultation with our workplace consultative forum, including union representatives. I think there were multiple avenues of communication, including all-staff messaging.

Senator RUSTON: Is the 312 the total number that you're expecting to take this up, or is there still further opportunity for staff to do it?

Ms Connolly : There's always opportunity for voluntary redundancies, as part of normal management action, but the broader call for the expressions of interest process has closed.

Senator RUSTON: That applies to that particular call, but if somebody wanted to do it at any time that is something that's open to all.

Mr Lye : For clarity, I think Ms Connolly said we're kind of at the right number of staffing for our budget. We don't expect to do a similar expression of interest process going forward, because we're now at the right staffing to manage our resources.

Senator RUSTON: No proactive action. With these voluntary redundancies, was there any pattern in terms of them coming from a particular branch or division?

Ms Connolly : No. They were spread across the department, and it was an open call for expressions of interest. I believe there was a relatively larger proportion from the Community Grants Hub; they are a large part of our workforce.

Senator RUSTON: You wouldn't say that was disproportionate for the number of people that worked there; it would be proportional.

Ms Connolly : I think it was slightly higher, but not materially.

Senator RUSTON: Was the process open to all levels of staff?

Ms Connolly : Yes.

Senator RUSTON: In the process of trying to fit everything into meeting your budget and your staffing numbers accordingly, has there been any internal reassignment of duties in the process of trying to meet your requirements?

Ms Connolly : The department has conducted a pretty granular approach to making sure that our resources are deployed where we need them in order to deliver our priorities. This committee has heard evidence in previous sessions about our keep-stop-start exercise, where we looked at: What do we need to keep doing? What can we stop doing? And what do we need to start doing in order to deliver on government priorities and the department's impact strategy? There have been a range of changes in the department as a result of that exercise but also normal management action following MYEFO and budget where we have measures. There have been some changes in the department in terms of where resources are allocated. There have been some small elements of restructuring in the department as well.

Senator RUSTON: There's nothing outside of business as usual in terms of the processes around that internal reassignment of—

Ms Connolly : I'd categorise it as regular management and leadership action.

Senator RUSTON: You would?

Ms Connolly : Yes.

Senator RUSTON: Okay. There was no direction to reassign staff?

Ms Connolly : No.

Senator RUSTON: In terms of the movement of staff within the agency, have there been any branches that have been underresourced that you've had to move people to or overresourced that you've had to move people out of?

Ms Connolly : Well, yes—

Senator RUSTON: Apart from in a small way. I mean in any substantial way.

Ms Connolly : We do always try to make sure that the resourcing is aligned to the work effort. For example, in my substantive division, we have moved from four branches down to three, which meant some consolidation of leadership reflecting that, post-MOG, the financial and information services group needed to be slightly smaller.

Senator RUSTON: Of those four branches, which was the one that was sort of abolished?

Ms Connolly : We had a dedicated financial statements branch, and the work of that branch was moved into both our Budget Development branch and our Financial Management branch.

Senator RUSTON: The roles and responsibilities of the people who were in the financial statements branch remained the same; they just got moved.

Ms Connolly : Yes.

Senator RUSTON: I'll go back to my original question around that. Apart from the MOG exercise that's gone on here, there was no significant move one way or the other amongst branches. It was just standard business as usual, trying to keep everything where it should be.

Mr Lye : The main priority has been to make sure our resources are in areas that are aligned to the priorities the department's identified. We call it the impact strategy. It's so they are aligned to where we think we need to try and put more effort. It's also aligned to the government's priorities around areas where they see that we need to try and make a difference. We're currently in consultation around the second action plan for family, domestic and sexual violence. We're looking very closely at the resourcing there to make sure that we've got sufficient people working on that process, because it involves not just policy development but consultation with stakeholders.

Senator RUSTON: I suppose part of my question is: have there been significant staff movements to align with the changes in the outputs that are being prioritised by the department and, clearly, as a result of government policy?

Mr Lye : I wouldn't say it's significant. I think, with the changes in the service delivery space where we have seen, as Ms Connolly said, a probably slightly higher number of voluntary redundancies, we're looking really closely at how we do that really well and the workforce we need to do that job.

Senator RUSTON: Back on the voluntary redundancies, I'm assuming from your answers that it was planned.

Ms Connolly : Yes.

Senator RUSTON: You're saying it was done in order to return to budget neutrality in terms of your FTE number.

Ms Connolly : That's right.

Senator RUSTON: There were no savings to be achieved from reducing the numbers, in the sense that you were actually just trying to stop a continued deficit.

Ms Connolly : That's right. There were some additional costs incurred in the current year as a result of the voluntary redundancy exercise, but it means that we will have a balanced budget next year.

Senator RUSTON: Has the minister's office requested verbally or in writing or have you delivered any information regarding terminating or amending employment contracts of any employees within the department or the portfolio agencies?

Ms Connolly : Not that I'm aware of.

Mr Lye : No. We keep the minister and the office apprised of the voluntary redundancy process and key changes we're making, but there's a pretty clear boundary between what they do and the management of the department. They don't get involved in that.

Senator RUSTON: And the assistant minister or her office?

Mr Lye : It's the same.

Senator RUSTON: Thanks.

ACTING CHAIR: We'll go to Senator Waters.

Senator WATERS: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Minister. I've got some questions about funding or rather the lack of funding for frontline services under the National Plan to End Violence Against Women and Children. Have we got the right people here on that?

Mr Lye : They will come for outcome 2. I think that's after lunch.

Senator WATERS: I thought they fitted better here. Maybe I'll make a start. It's a question about measuring unmet need in frontline services. There has been a program that the department has funded through the AIHW for many, many years. I asked them last night: When is your end date? When are we going to get a measure of unmet need for how many women and children are turned away from frontline family, domestic and sexual violence services? They didn't have an end date, so my question is, firstly: when are the Commonwealth going to know just how many women and children are being turned back to violence, so that they can have better information to decide whether to fix that problem or not?

Mr Lye : The officials who are involved with that project—I know the one you're talking about—are from outcome 2.

Senator WATERS: There's nothing you can tell me now? I thought it belonged in this session.

Mr Lye : I would be unhelpful.

ACTING CHAIR: I think outcome 2 would be a better fit because you're going to the detail of that.

Senator WATERS: Perhaps it's a question for the minister. How is the government deciding how much money to allocate or not allocate to frontline services if you don't even know how much unmet need there is—how many women and children are being turned away from help when they seek it? How do you make your funding decisions?

Senator Chisholm: Obviously, I need some help from the department in terms of answering the details on that, which I understand will be available later. But I do know that, as a government, we've put a record investment into family and domestic violence services and the support that the Commonwealth government provides. That's something that's been built up over the three years that we've been in government, and we continue to deliver record amounts of funding to do what we can as a government to deal with these matters because they are of national significance. I expect that the department will be able to provide more information for you when those responsible for those matters are on later this afternoon.

Senator WATERS: Just going to that budget figure—certainly there's been an increase in investment compared to the previous government over the last several years. It's still, according to the women's safety sector, not enough and not enabling them to help everyone. I really couldn't see much in this current budget for frontline services. There was a small top-up for workers, which of course is welcome, but it's essentially just inflation. I know the government tries to dine out on saying that it's increased funding historically. I'm not disputing that. But what is in this budget that is going to go to frontline services? Can someone run me through that, please.

Mr Lye : We're currently out in consultation with the family, domestic and sexual violence sector, and that's for the second action plan, so it would be incongruous for us to announce policies when we haven't talked to stakeholders about that. There are things that have been done since the government has been in government. In the recent budget, we have a significant increase in our children and families services. Obviously the states and territories are primarily delivering front-door services in the family, domestic and sexual violence space—

Senator WATERS: Using federal money.

Mr Lye : Yes—using some of our federal funding. We directly commission services in the children and family space. I think it's fair to say that that general children and family sector also provides services to families. They could come with any issue that's affecting the family, and that includes family, domestic and sexual violence. That's a very large program, which received a funding boost in the budget. Again, I think officials in outcome 2 could talk to that and give you that context alongside the work that's happening around the second action plan, which goes directly to your question.

Senator WATERS: The second action plan won't be in place until 2027-28. I hope you're not implying that there won't be an increase in funding for frontline services until then.

Mr Lye : I'm not implying that.

Senator WATERS: You said that you couldn't answer that, because it would be premature because that process was underway. How does that make sense?

Mr Lye : The process is happening right now. I think the consultations began last week. That's ongoing intensively over the next four to five months.

Senator WATERS: But my question was: how much money is going to frontline services in this budget? You said they're consulting on the second plan, which won't be finished for years. I'm still interested in the primary question.

Mr Lye : I'm saying to you that the officials can come and give you the detail in outcome 2.

Senator WATERS: Okay. I'm interested also in how you define frontline services and whether you're including 1800RESPECT in that, which I would query because it's a mere referral service. It does important work, but it's not actually providing frontline services. It's just effectively directing people to other underfunded existing services. Do you include funding for 1800RESPECT in your definition of frontline services?

Mr Lye : I understand the point you're making about referral versus intensive interventions, but it is a frontline service. There's no doubt it's a frontline service.

Senator WATERS: So you do include that?

Mr Lye : Well, the officials can come and give you the answers to those questions in outcome 2.

Senator WATERS: Okay. My last question is: do you include the leaving violence payments in your definition of funding for frontline services?

Mr Lye : I would just say to you, again, that the Leaving Violence Program can involve referrals and other arrangements, so it is definitely frontline in character. It's also principally a payment that goes to people as well. So, if your concern is that somehow the Leaving Violence Program and 1800RESPECT might be used to argue that we don't need to increase frontline services, in terms of those traditional FDSV services, I don't think that that is in any way what we're up to. But if you want to recognise who is at the front line, in terms of how equipped our workforce are or what sort of skillsets they have, then it's very definitely frontline.

Senator WATERS: It's more about falsely implying that you're funding the front line when you're actually funding these other important services that actually aren't delivering frontline support.

Mr Lye : I understand what you're saying. There's just no question that these, in my mind, are very much frontline services. But that doesn't negate the fact that we need to have sufficient frontline services that provide more intensive case managed interventions with families experiencing FDSV.

Senator WATERS: Thank you.

ACTING CHAIR: Senator Ruston.

Senator RUSTON: I just have a few questions about the department's use of artificial intelligence. On the department's website, it states:

Currently, our approved AI use cases are within the:

Service delivery, Policy and legal and Corporate and enabling domains …

Does the department use AI to generate policy briefs?

Ms Connolly : The department uses AI to do two things: it uses AI to enhance personal productivity, and we are also venturing into using AI to enhance our service delivery. In terms of generating policy ideas, no, we don't use AI for generating policy ideas. We do use AI for reviewing reports, consolidating data and perhaps extracting some insights, but, ultimately, a human is the person who interprets the outputs from various prompts from a Microsoft Copilot chat, which is our primary AI tool, and then formulates and prepares the policy advice.

Senator RUSTON: I take it that the salient point out of that is: not for policy ideas.

Ms Connolly : No.

Senator RUSTON: Okay. The department's website also states:

Staff mainly use AI systems for:

…   …   …

drafting and reviewing policy documents for clarity and compliance …

I'm wondering if you could explain what you mean by 'compliance'. Compliance with what?

Ms Connolly : It might be that you have a rule set, like the Commonwealth Procurement Rules, and it's open to an officer to put some draft tender documentation together and say, 'Do you think that this aligns with the Commonwealth Procurement Rules?' But ultimately, again, it's a matter for the delegate to confirm that the compliance is correct, rather than relying on artificial intelligence.

Senator RUSTON: So there is human oversight, so the person who actually uses the AI still remains responsible for the recommendations and the actions they take in relation to that?

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Okay.

Mr Lye : Senator, Ms Power might take you through that DPO change. Obviously, she's just given you what the existing legislation says, and the budget measure will change arrangements.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Thank you.

Ms Power : Certainly. Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Obviously, these are reasonable arrangements, you consider—and they have failed at all to pay any debt in that time; is that correct?

Ms Power : It will be people who have a debt over $10,000. Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Nonlodgement of tax returns is one of the things that I and my colleagues hear about a lot when it comes to child support and outstanding debts. How many parents engaged in the child support system are recorded as not having lodged their tax return?

Ms Power : Services Australia makes around 150,000 referrals a year to the ATO for child support parents for non-lodgement of tax returns.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Can you please tell us how many of those would be for a single financial year, two financial years, three years and so on. That might have to be taken on notice.

ACTING CHAIR: Senator, we're going to rotate when you find a useful break, just to give Senator O'Sullivan a quick round of questions before he has to go back.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Sure. I am trying to understand how many parents in the system are now non-lodgers and the number of cases where this is a repeat offence.

Mr Lye : Again, there was a measure in the budget around this as well, to provide resources to the ATO to chase more of these non-lodgers.

Ms Power : Services Australia, which administers the Child Support Scheme, does not have direct powers to require people to lodge a tax return. Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Okay. When it comes to the weaponisation of child support—parents refusing to pay their child support in order to cause financial harm to another parent—what policies or legislation are in place now to address this particular issue?

Ms Power : I can speak to the measures that were announced in the recent budget package, and there are a range of measures through the budget package that go to weaponisation of the Child Support Scheme, which we know is an issue that has been recently raised, in particular, by the Commonwealth Ombudsman in his report, Weaponisingchild support: when the system fails families. Two of the key measures that have been announced in the budget go to known ways that the system is weaponised. This is the open exchange of information requirement, which is part of the change of assessment process. When people want to seek a change to their child support assessment, they apply for a change of assessment. As part of the change of assessment process under current arrangements, both parties are required to provide a range of detailed financial and other information to support the process. It's been identified by the Ombudsman and others that this can be exploited by perpetrators of family and domestic violence to try to seek information about their partners or to harass them, so the budget package commits $10 million to remove the mandatory open exchange of information process and replace it with a process that will be managed by Services Australia, whereby they will able to determine what information is required to be provided, providing better protections for parents' information and income as well as those protections against harassment. There are also new powers for the Child Support Registrar to be able to not make decisions or refuse objections when those objections are made vexatiously or with the predominant purpose of harassing or abusing a parent. That is the range of new powers that we are exploring there, and probably some key examples.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: One of the significant consequences of non-payment of child support is the flow-on impact that it has on people in receipt of family tax benefit part A, with debts created for parents, despite the child support not being received. Ms Power : Yes, at a high level. This is particularly the case in private collect cases, or where people have a private collection arrangement. As Mr Flavel mentioned before, the government doesn't have visibility of whether payments are made or not in a private collection arrangement, because it's fundamentally a direct transfer between two private individuals. When we are calculating payments, or family tax benefit entitlements, there is a connection between child support and family payments, and in the private collect system people are assumed to have received their child support payments from their partner when calculating their family tax benefit debt. That may or may not have happened in practice and, if there is a change to your child support assessment and you're receiving more child support income, that can lead to a reduction in your family tax benefit entitlement, which can have impacts on paying parents or payee parents in particular.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: The Commonwealth Ombudsman report noted that the legislation is weak here because a parent can accrue a debt through no fault their own and that there is no legal mechanism to waive the debt in these circumstances, particularly as it relates to weaponisation. What changes have been made to the legislation to correct this?

Ms Power : There is, in some instances, an existing mechanism available that can be used to, in effect, remove that debt. In cases where there is evidence of family and domestic violence or financial abuse, a person can apply for a partial exemption from the maintenance action test. The partial exemption is used in situations where it would be unreasonable to expect a parent to collect their child support payments. In that instance, the value of the FTB debt would be recalculated having excluded those payments, which in effect removes the FTB debt.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: The Commonwealth Ombudsman report Weaponisingchild support: when the system fails families made eight recommendations. Can you please provide an update on the implementation status of each of those recommendations?

Ms Power : I think seven out of the eight recommendations that the Ombudsman made are the responsibility of Services Australia, because they go to service delivery practices. Services Australia, I understand, is working quite hard on implementation of those recommendations, but questions would be best directed to them.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: That report identified that the legislation for child support was unhelpful when it comes to collection enforcement powers where financial abuse is taking place—for example, to garnish money from third parties, intercept tax returns or use departure prohibition orders. Where are you up to with changing the legislation to strengthen these powers, or is that another concern of Services Australia?

Ms Power : No, as we've mentioned, there are a number of enforcement powers available, and it has been announced that they will be strengthened in the recent budget package. There is also funding around tax lodgement and prosecutions related to tax lodgement. Legislation will need to be progressed for both the departure prohibition orders and the employer withholding measures, and we are working on preparing that legislation at the moment.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Recommendation 7 of that report made some specific recommendations on what changes should be made to the legislation, yet DSS only noted the recommendation. Does this mean you won't be making the changes?

Mr Flavel : I think I would just reiterate what the secretary and Ms Power have said, which is that the budget package of measures on child support is probably one of the most significant changes we've seen to child support legislation in the last couple of decades, with the sole purpose of driving out weaponisation in the system. That's very significant. We know from the statistics that around 100,000 parents in the child support system have a family and domestic violence tag attached to their file, and probably, in reality, the number of people experiencing FDV is higher than that. Therefore, dealing with weaponisation in all its forms is really important. We have talked about some of the measures but some of the other things in the $180-odd million package are giving parents a greater level of visibility over the risks and benefits of private collect versus agency collect, dealing with international child support cases and a range of other measures, all aimed at driving out weaponisation. The legislation is obviously still to come, but it substantively deals with a lot of the issues the Ombudsman had in that recommendation in this report.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Recommendation 8 of the report, which both DSS and Services Australia accepted, sought a comprehensive update within 12 months of the day of the report. The date of that report was June 2025, meaning the update is due now. Can we expect to see that provided to the Commonwealth Ombudsman and published any time soon?

Ms Power : We're working with Services Australia to finalise that input at the moment.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Thank you.

Mr Lye : We spoke to the Ombudsman ahead of the budget about the package of measures and took him through that. That set of child support measures that Mr Flavel talked about directly responds to his report. It's the government's response to many of the issues that he has raised.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: The measures in this year's budget don't appear to address these most significant legislative deficiencies. Is there a reason they haven't been included in the package? Were they costed? Which of the measures in the budget will require legislative changes?

Ms Power : A number of the measures recommended by the Ombudsman are in the budget package. Removal of the open exchange of information is an example of that. There are also a number of changes contained in the budget package which don't align exactly with the recommendation made by the Commonwealth Ombudsman but that have a similar effect, without some of the potential further impacts that these recommendations might have had.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: I just want to go through those measures in the budget package. There is $13.6 million for a collection arrangement guidance tool. What is this tool? I'm assuming it's an online tool, is it?

Ms Power : I'm happy to speak to that. The collection arrangement guidance tool is intended to go to an issue that's been identified through some of the research that we have conducted, as part of the government's response to the family law inquiry, that found that parents, when they're entering the child support system, don't always have a clear understanding of the two different collection arrangements available to them; that is, entering into a private collect arrangement where parents transfer child support directly between them or into an agency collect arrangement where Services Australia facilitates payment between parents. There are a number of different risks and benefits associated with those two collection arrangements and different risks of weaponisation or different ways that those arrangements can be weaponised that have consequences for people's child support and whether it's received down the track. The idea of the online collection arrangement guidance tool is that it will be embedded within the online application process, which is the way that most people apply for child support, but we also expect that, for the small number of people who apply either by the telephone or through the office, they will be run through that tool as part of their application process. It will ask a series of risk-screening questions, which will go to things like whether there has been presence of family domestic violence in the relationship previously and whether people are known to lodge their tax returns on time. On the basis of parents' answers to those risk-screening questions, the tool will provide tailored advice on some of the risks and benefits of those collection options to enable parents to make the most informed decision that they can about which collection arrangement will be most appropriate for them.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Thank you. I suppose $13.6 million is a lot of money for something online. You've provided some detail. Are there any more components of this that you can explain to us? How many staff were part of the costing? Was there any capex or opex expenditure, for example?

Ms Power : I don't have that detail at hand, but it's a significant ICT build that will be required to put the process in place. There will also be a range of further outreach and communication to parents as part of the process. For instance, if a parent flags a number of risk-screening questions but still chooses an arrangement that might have a very high level of risk for them, there will be follow-up communications to them at various points down the track and outreach, and there are costs associated with that ongoing communication as well.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: The implementation time for this measure is not until 1 January 2028, so why is it taking 18 months to build?

Ms Power : We're really conscious of the need, with tools like this, to have a close understanding of how they're going to work for parents. We are dealing with is a system that can be quite complex to understand and parents who are engaging with it are at a point of significant stress in their lives, so we'll be doing a significant amount of customer-centred, design with Services Australia, to make sure that the tool is as accessible and as usable as it can be for customers. We also want to make sure that we take the time to get that right so that the most useful tailored advice can be provided to parents to support them at that time.

That also includes what's known as reserved weeks—effectively, an encouragement of partners to share the leave by reserving four weeks of the 26 weeks for at least one of the partners to take. Senator O'SULLIVAN: To confirm, the 26 weeks or six months is a family pool, or a household pool.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: But a single parent could access 26 weeks.

Mr Flavel : That's correct, yes—so as not to bias a single parent.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: To be clear, the primary parent's entitlement is only increasing by five days, then, over the current amount?

Mr Flavel : Since 2023, that maximum has gone from 18 weeks to 22 weeks, so it's gone up by four weeks over the past three or four years.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: What's the actual gain, then, for the majority of mothers?

Mr Flavel : The gain is twofold. One is an overall increase in the level of government assistance on a family basis, regardless of whether you're talking about a couple family or a single family. There is also that sharing of the leave, which helps address some of the systemic biases towards it being, historically, mothers who would take time out of the workforce and suffer some of the consequences of that in terms of pay and in terms of superannuation to actually having a more shared arrangement for care, which is obviously beneficial to mothers.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: On Monday, the Prime Minister posted on Instagram claiming, 'From July, you'll get six months of paid parental leave,' but, as you've just confirmed, the secondary parent's four weeks are a 'use it or lose it' arrangement, meaning the vast majority of Australian mothers can actually access only 5.5 months, not 6 months. Is it right for the Prime Minister to say that you will get 26 weeks?

Mr Flavel : There are 26 weeks available for a family, as I said.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: If you're a single parent, you'll get 26 weeks, but if you're not—

Mr Flavel : A family gets 26 weeks, and the family includes, in this particular example you're running with, a mother. Therefore, it's beneficial to the mother, regardless of whether the mother is actually taking those weeks, because, of course, it's an entitlement that is going to the family in that particular instance, with benefits to the mother.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: But it's a very restrictive entitlement, isn't it? What's the rationale? Why wouldn't you say to a family, 'You've got 26 weeks; how you apportion it will be up to you'? The government is actually mandating how a family would apportion the leave. It's use it or lose it for the secondary parent, so it's not right to say that it's 26 weeks when an individual can't actually take 26 weeks.

Mr Lye : It is right in terms of the family access to it. But you're saying that you think, for example, some fathers will not want to avail themselves of the four weeks?

Senator O'SULLIVAN: Some fathers can't. Just to be clear, I think it's terrific that parents, fathers in particular, are able to take paid parental leave. I want to be absolutely crystal clear about that. But why are we not actually just empowering the parents, the family, to decide how to apportion that? For those that can't, such as a family where dad's running a small business and taking that time is just not practical at all, or whatever their circumstance might be, this is limited, and it's not right, Minister, for the Prime Minister to say, 'You will now have 26 weeks of paid parental leave,' when it's 'if it suits your arrangement'.

Senator Chisholm: I think you're being a bit pedantic there, Senator O'Sullivan. I think the department's witnesses have talked through the circumstances of where it applies. What the Prime Minister says is accurate, and I understand that some people may be in different circumstances, but the opportunity is there.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: If it suits you—there are lots of people it doesn't suit. You need to have a look at the post that the Prime Minister posted and have a look at the response from families.

Mr Lye : I look at everything the Prime Minister posts.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: Did you see the comments on his post? It might not please you too much to look at every one of them. Was the impact on coupled families ever considered when designing this policy? Why was the use-it-or-lose-it feature chosen over simply giving families the choice to allocate those weeks how they see fit?

Mr Flavel : It was based on evidence, including looking at international evidence. Obviously, many other countries have paid parental leave. In the absence of use it or lose it, the evidence shows that you get a default position of the mother taking all of the leave, and what that does is reinforce gender stereotypes about the mother taking the time off and therefore, as I said, the resultant impacts on lifetime earnings and superannuation. It is quite deliberate, based on the evidence that shows that, if you use it or lose it, by very definition, some people will not use it. But it is a feature designed to ensure that there is gender-neutral or gender-based sharing, or sharing across a couple of the care when the government is providing paid parental leave.

Mr Lye : Also, the scheme sits alongside provision of employer paid parental leave, so the illustration that you gave is precisely the area where a government scheme can step in where a person might otherwise not have access to any payment for a period of time to have off work. It actually does tend to fill that gap and provide an opportunity for people to spend time with their young child after the birth.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: As I've stated, I 100-per-cent encourage and support secondary parents—if that's the right terminology, the other parent—to take time off work in those early months of a child's life. Obviously, it's a wonderful thing and a wonderful opportunity that people should be encouraged to take up, but this is actually saying to families, 'Government know best; we know best for how you will make your arrangements.' Why would you not consider just making the full 26 weeks available and how they want to allocate it is up to them? Of course, encourage fathers to take that leave, but, if that's not for them, why penalise the household when that might not be an option for them?

Mr Flavel : I just refer back to what I said earlier, which is that the hard evidence on this suggests that, in that model of unlimited choice, if you want to call it that, you just get a bias towards the mother.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: Have they had that choice before?

Mr Flavel : This is just based on evidence from overseas and other examples of where you have provided this leave—

Senator O'SULLIVAN: Can you provide that evidence?

Mr Flavel : Yes, I'm very happy to. I'm pretty sure—although somebody will correct me if I'm wrong—that the Women's Economic Equality Taskforce actually looked at this issue and actually made a recommendation, based on that evidence, to have a kind of use-it-or-lose-it or reserved weeks model to deal with that known bias.

Senator Chisholm: I believe the coalition implemented it when in government as well. They had a two weeks use-it-or-lose-it provision.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: I refer to the Prime Minister's post. The majority of the comments—or perhaps all the comments on there—criticising this use-it-or-lose-it clause are actually from mothers.

Senator Chisholm: You are criticising your own policy there as well.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: The next measure I want to ask questions on is the $64.9 million to provide greater protections for parents in private collection arrangements. Can you break down the costing for this measure, please?

Ms Power : Certainly. There are three components to this measure, all of which are designed to either provide further pathways into agency collect for private collect parents or to provide greater protections for parents when they're in private collect. One of the measures is to allow payer parents who are paying child support to choose an agency collect arrangement if they want to do so. The reason for this is that around 21 per cent of people in the child support scheme who have a family and domestic violence indicator are payer parents, and, at present, the payee has all choice over which collection arrangement you're in. In some instances, a payee might choose a private collect arrangement against the wishes of the payer in order to maintain ongoing contact with their former partner, so this new option will provide a greater protection for payer parents who are experiencing family domestic violence to enter an arrangement that's more arm's length from their former partner or from the second parent. There are also changes to allow parents who moved from private collect into agency collect to bring a larger amount of child support arrears into the agency collect scheme for collection by Services Australia and changes that will allow parents who are in private collect and receive a family tax benefit debt, as we discussed earlier, to be able to pause collection of the family tax benefit debt for three months to allow them extra time to collect the child support debt that has been raised or to put other arrangements in place to manage that family tax benefit debt.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: How many parents have you modelled in the costing to switch over to agency collect from private collection arrangements?

Ms Power : I don't have that information at hand, but we do have it available and I'm very happy to provide it on notice.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Okay. How, specifically, will this help improve debt collection, given we have such a large number of cases with debt now? Won't this just add to the case load? I just want to clarify an example. If a parent is in a private arrangement today, but the paying parent is not making the payments, the receiving parent can call and switch over to agency collection, but any debt that might be owed can't be acted on until the switch to agency collect is made. Is that correct?

Ms Power : Yes. Services Australia doesn't have a role in collecting child support debt for people in private collect arrangements, so it's not until the person moves into an agency collect arrangement that they would be able to get that support collecting the debt—because, I guess, the crux of a private collect arrangement is that the government is not a party to that arrangement.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: You mentioned that the measure also includes the ability to delay the collection of FTB debt for three months, but it won't waive the debt, so the parent would still need to pay the debt; it just gives them more time to put arrangements in place. Is that correct?

Ms Power : There is a range of options that they could take under that circumstance. In the first instance, the parent could just have more time in order to be able to actually collect that debt from the other parent, but they may also, in that period, choose to move into an agency collect arrangement where they would be able to get support to collect that debt from Services Australia. At the point that they move into an agency collect arrangement, their FTB debt would also be recalculated, because, in agency collect, your FTB entitlement is based on the child support you've actually received rather than an assumption that you have received child support that you may or may not have received. Your family tax benefit entitlement would then be based on, as I said, child support you've received. If you hadn't received that child support, then the debt would be removed until you received child support. The other option that could be put in place at that point is that a parent could apply for a partial exemption from the maintenance action test, which I think we also referred to earlier. This could be used if there was a situation where the FTB debt had occurred as a result of financial abuse, coercion or family and domestic violence, and a partial exemption in that instance would, in effect, waive the family tax benefit debt. So it would be as though that debt had not existed.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Can you detail for us, please, this commitment of $9.7 million to improve online services and communications.

Ms Power : Absolutely. This also goes to that interaction between the child support and family tax benefit systems. For a family to be able to receive the higher rate of family tax benefit, family tax benefit part A, they are required to satisfy the maintenance action test, which requires a parent to have applied for child support. We know from research in 2019 that around 60 per cent of women were not informed of the differences between child support payment collection options and the implications for the FTB payments, and we've seen similar findings as part of the survey of separated parents, which the department undertook as part of the government's response to the family law inquiry. There are, in some instances, low levels of understanding amongst parents around what the maintenance action test is and the need to satisfy it to receive those higher rates of family tax benefit. This policy, $9.7 million, is intended to address that by providing more and easier to understand information to parents, at the point that they're applying for family payments, to understand what the maintenance action test is and how to satisfy it. As part of their application process for family payments, they'll be able to indicate whether or not they've satisfied the maintenance action test and, if they haven't, the reason for that. The policy will also fund additional outreach. For a parent who might have said, for instance, 'I can't satisfy the maintenance action test. I can't apply for child support because I'm concerned that will present a risk to my safety,' there would then be outreach from a Services Australia social worker to understand the person's circumstance and speak to them about the options that might be available, and that could include applying for an exemption from the maintenance action test, which allows you to then continue to receive the higher rate of family tax benefit. We expect that this investment of $9.7 million, which will improve service delivery, will lead to more people satisfying the maintenance action test in the first instance, and also more people who need an exemption from the maintenance action test being able to receive one.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: There is a further $10 million for change of assessments and objections. Can you provide the funding breakdown for this measure as well, please?

Ms Power : The $10 million refers to the removal of the open exchange of information requirement. The cost there is partly ICT but also funding for Services Australia. Because we'll be removing the automatic requirement that all information provided in an open exchange of information process is automatically provided to the other partner, there will be a more intensive process for Services Australia to have to review that information, determine what information is required to be provided, or to summarise it in some instances. I think the majority of that $10 million will support that work by Services Australia to facilitate that new information exchange.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: There is $3.6 million for Services Australia to identify systems abuse. What is this funding for? Is this just staffing?

Ms Power : This goes to the additional powers for the registrar, which I touched on briefly earlier. Legislative changes will be put in place so that, from 1 July 2027, the Child Support Registrar will be able to refuse certain applications and notifications where they're made for the purpose of harassing the other parent, with new discretionary powers to refuse vexatious change of assessment applications, to refuse to accept a child support application if it's being made to harass a recipient who would be a payee anyway, and to disallow an objection that has no merit without involving the other party. We expect that these powers will be used only in quite specific circumstances where there's quite clear harassment or weaponisation of the system occurring. In some instances, management of these cases and the new legislation will require quite intensive engagement from Services Australia, so the costs there predominantly relate to those service delivery needs.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: There is $6.1 million for the ATO to prosecute parents who repeatedly fail to submit a tax return. Can you provide the funding breakdown? for that, please?

Ms Power : I don't have a further breakdown beyond that. It's an ATO measure, but it does, as you said, support prosecution of parents for repeated non-lodgement.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: In a policy sense, what does 'repeatedly' mean? Will it be one financial year, two or more, and what will the threshold be for the ATO to take action?

Ms Power : That is a question you would need to direct to the ATO or Services Australia.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: What is involved in prosecuting parents?

Ms Power : Once again, that is a question you'll need to direct to the ATO.

Ms Power : This is not so much for improvements to Single Touch Payroll as it exists but to expand its use in new purposes by Services Australia. Single Touch Payroll information will be used to validate income estimates for parents and to flag more quickly where those estimates are wrong. Single Touch Payroll data is already used in some aspects of the child support system by Services Australia. This will just expand the use of that information to new purposes to make sure that people's income estimates, and therefore their child support assessments, are more accurate.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: The budget measure fact sheet on your website states on page 2 that around half of the 70,000 income estimates lodged each year are incorrect. Are they maliciously or intentionally incorrect?

Ms Power : We don't know. It would likely be a combination of both.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Is there a way of getting that information?

ACTING CHAIR: Could you step us through what you see as the most important changes that we've seen from the budget in your department?

Mr Lye : In this outcome, undoubtedly the child support changes, which we talked a little bit about earlier. I might get Mr Flavel to run through the central features of that change. It's a really important reform of a scheme that hasn't been exposed to a lot of reform over the years. This is a really substantial change, and principally to try to address weaponisation of the scheme and to pay better attention to family, domestic and sexual violence, which is present in the child support scheme and responsible for some of the problems that we see in it. I'll let Mr Flavel give you an overview.

Mr Flavel : I think Ms Power did a stellar job earlier of describing most of the bits of the package, so it would be hard to top that. But I will just reinforce some points from earlier. We have more than 100,000 parents in the system who have a family and domestic violence indicator attached to their file. And of course that's only where it's reported or known to Services Australia. So I think it would be a reasonable assumption that levels of FDV or the potential for violence are much higher than that. Intuitively, if you think about Commonwealth systems and potential for abuse, child support is going to be one of the top, if not the most—just given the nature of it being a payment between two individuals who've separated. Therefore these are really significant and substantial and important reforms.

Speaking over a reasonably long period, I've not seen as much ambition in terms of really tackling weaponisation in such a way, which is important, and it is important for us to implement in a way that brings stakeholders along and actually achieves the outcomes. What we are interested in here is actually seeing rates of weaponisation and abuse decline. The thing about the package is there are a lot of different elements that all go to the core issue of weaponisation, both the direct—things like removing the automatic exchange of information. Not only does that expose some people to unnecessary risk by giving information about bank statements and other personal detail but also we know that there's a large number of people who would apply for a child support reassessment but don't because they don't want to expose themselves to that risk. So it's important not only to drive better outcomes for people using it but also to get people the right amount.

A lot of the measures we talked about before—about getting people to lodge their tax returns on time, using single-touch payroll to get more accurate income assessments, and then using employer withholding to get payments more on time and in a more systematic way. And then a lot of the changes are around ensuring that people understand when they make a choice. Fifty per cent of people go into agency collect and 50 per cent into private collect. But we know from some of the research we've done that when parents go into private collect, they often have an inferior outcome; they don't get the payment. There's no ability, because it's a private arrangement, to have any kind of government assistance. But they do fear going into agency collect because they don't want to have another front opening up with their ex-partner. And that of course leads to terrible outcomes for them and, more importantly, terrible outcomes for the children. We always orient ourselves around the child support system not being about the two parents but actually about improving the wellbeing of children. We know rates of child poverty are much higher for children in child support families than they are in the rest of the community. So we should care a lot about fixing up these systems.

Some of the other changes, like some of the international agreements, as I mentioned earlier—the situation where some parents, primarily fathers, in Australia have children overseas and then the mothers cannot get access to child support. It's a pretty awful outcome. So changes that are being made to allow direct access to our system are really important too. So there's a lot to do and I'm not doing it justice by just skating across, but I did want to underscore how significant the package is. Thinking about efforts the government's made to drive out weaponisation more generally, this represents one of the most significant bits along the way in terms of showing seriousness about it. But, as I said, it really comes down to then legislating, implementing and actually getting the outcomes we want to see.

Senator RUSTON: I'm interested in your views in relation to child safety specifically. Does the child placement principle ever prevent removal of a child from a physically unsafe environment?

Ms Hunter : No. The child placement principle takes into account safety; it sits alongside safety. I believe you can't have one without the other. It's about where the child is being placed. There's a hierarchy of where the child needs to be placed. If it's not followed, there is a risk of the child losing their identity of who they are, as an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander child being totally removed from community. That's a safety issue as well as a concern. Sometimes children have to be removed, and sometimes they've gone through the placement and there isn't a place for the child in that hierarchy, but, more often than not, there is. I don't think it's either/or; it's together.

Senator RUSTON: Does the child placement principle prevent the removal if the physical environment is unsafe? To that end, should it be made explicit in the legislation that that is the case that a child can be removed or that the principle can't prevent the child from being removed?

Ms Hunter : The principle doesn't prevent the child from being removed.

Senator RUSTON: Do you think it could be or should be explicit in legislation?

Ms Hunter : I don't know if it has to be in legislation. I think there needs to be more education around what the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Child Placement Principle is and the five elements of that. We just recently put up a social media tile on what it is, and maybe that's something we could undertake around educating people on exactly what that is. I don't think the legislation needs to say it explicitly, because, if you understand the child placement principle, then you would understand that that's not the case.

Senator RUSTON: But there's the case of the other side of the argument. What's the harm of putting it in there? It comes to this question: do you agree that cultural connection must never become an excuse for tolerating an unsafe environment for a child?

Ms Hunter : I don't think that's an argument to be had, really. I think if a child's unsafe, then a child needs to be removed. That's when we follow the child placement principle.

Ms Hunter : Yes.

Ms Hunter : I'm sorry?

Senator RUSTON: Do you think courts and caseworkers should be required to record expressly how risks of violence, sexual abuse, alcohol abuse, unsafe housing and all those very important elements have been assessed?

Senator RUSTON: Quite clearly, safety is absolutely paramount, so I'm interested in understanding why so many children continue, sadly, to be exposed to unsafe homes and violence and neglect. Do you have a view as to why we still hear and see such terrible stories of unsafe violence, neglect et cetera?

Ms Hunter : We need more investment in early intervention. If we have that going in the front end, then we have fewer kids coming in the back end. The risk assessments need to be documented exactly as they are and what that looks like. I believe that, if a child is removed, the work should be done on how reunification is to happen. Every child—and I've worked in out-of-home care for a very long time—I've spoken to or who has been removed wants their family. So how do we make the family safe? We can't just remove kids, and then, when they turn 18, they find their way home. If we remove children, we should be looking at the start of how we work with the family to get these children back home.

Senator RUSTON: I suppose the other side of it is that there are families who have publicly made statements that they believe cultural principles have been used to justify leaving children in unsafe environments.

Ms Hunter : I would disagree. That's where we come back to understanding those assessments of children. Children need to be connected to family to understand who they are and to build their identity and their sense of knowing. It doesn't mean sometimes you can't reunify a child, but are they still connected to their family? That would be my argument. If a child's unsafe and needs to be removed, that needs to be done. But how do we keep them connected to who they are as a person that has a family?

Senator RUSTON: I probably know the answer to this, but do you think that there needs to be a better and a clearer explanation and understanding of how child placement principles protect safety in practice so the public has a better understanding of how this principle works, what it's seeking to achieve, with greater clarity about the protection mechanisms that you've just spoken about that actually do exist?

Ms Hunter : Yes, I agree with that. I think we also need to make sure that practitioners—and I've been a practitioner, so I'm not blaming them—have a better understanding of why as well. I think they're at the forefront about risk assessments, making sure that they've done the risk assessment, understanding not only the Aboriginal child placement principle but also risk. There's another element to this. There's the matter of, if a child goes into care, whether they safer being in care. There's a whole other argument about that as well. Ms Hunter : I think it's a combination of both. If you look, in every state and territory it's implemented differently. It depends on which state you're in if you have to or you may.
